title: This 'British' ferry is run by a Kochi temple & it's free for students
content: Kochi: Every morning, Anil wheels his motorbike onto the steel deck of a passenger boat named 'Sree Mayilvahanam' at Kunjithai jetty near North Paravur. He hands over 12 and watches the boat glide across the Kochi–Kottappuram canal in Periyar toward Pallipuram. In barely five minutes, he is across, heading toward his work at the Munambam fishing harbour. By road, that journey would mean a 14-km detour through heavy traffic via Moothakunnam, taking half an hour and far more fuel. By ferry, I reach the other side in five or six minutes. Otherwise, it's a long, frustrating ride all the way around, Anil says. For generations along northern Vypin island, this waterway has been an unavoidable boundary. Known locally as British Kadathu (British Ferry), the crossing predates the motorised ferry by decades, tracing back to when Travancore and Cochin were separate princely states. Today, this public lifeline is owned, fuelled, and operated by a temple committee in Kunjithai that first took it at auction to raise money for a larger shrine. Over nearly three decades, the temple and the ferry have grown side by side, sustained by the same community. A crossing through history Long before engines arrived, commuters crossed in small wooden canoes - V V Vidyadharan, secretary of the Sree Balasubrahmanya Swami Kshetra Kshema Sangham, which now runs the boat, recalls elders describe the time when the waterway marked the formal customs frontier between Travancore and Cochin. Goods were subject to strict inspection and levies, particularly salt. Royal postal runners (anchalottakkaran) sprinted along the banks ringing brass bells, asking people to clear the road, while a border post checked cargo. The name British Kadathu was coined when the crossing was leased during colonial rule to link passengers and mail to the Murikkumpadam railway line across the border. Across the water, Pallipuram had evolved into an administrative centre under Portuguese, Dutch, and British administrations, home to a police station, registry office, and the historic Church of Our Lady of the Snows (Manju Matha Church), he told Onmanorama. Families depended on this crossing for everything, from administrative work to attending the church's annual feast (perunnal), says senior committee member K S Balakrishnan. Decades ago, when authorities proposed a bridge here, local landlords resisted land acquisition. The alignment was eventually shifted kilometres south to Cherai, leaving Kunjithai dependent on the water. A temple's gamble The temple's own origin traces back to a village crisis. P N Balakrishnan, the committee's oldest member, recalls a smallpox epidemic that struck the household of a prominent traditional midwife in the mid-1960s. The midwife died, and following a large post-funeral gathering, dozens of people fell severely ill with internal smallpox. Over twenty people in that single house were bedridden. An astrological divination revealed that ancient rituals dedicated to Lord Subrahmanya were stopped and had fallen into neglect on the land. Local youths gathered soil and bricks from neighbouring houses to build a modest shrine. The astrologer prophesied that within seven years, an adjacent 22-cent pond would be filled and a permanent temple would rise. That prophecy took physical shape as the Sree Balasubrahmanya Swami Temple, but maintaining it required steady funds. In the late 1990s, when the panchayat auctioned the ferry rights, the committee stepped in to secure revenue while providing a safer alternative to hazardous canoes. Around 1998–99, they won the contract with a bid of 31,100 for 20 months. The catch: they did not own a boat. We rented a vessel first just to test viability, Vidyadharan recalls. As passenger volume grew, members pooled savings; some even pawned their wives' gold wedding chains (thalimala)...
